People who make a living on it, okay... but gaming? I've been gaming exclusively on Windows since the late 90s. Even when I went through my Linux phases, I always had a Windows partition stashed away to game on. After Win10 hit, I made the leap: there's no machine on my network running Windows anymore, and besides one or two quirky Steam titles that just will not work with Wine, I am playing everything just as well as I did on Windows, and without any of the guilt.

It's absolutely doable. And while I recognize that doesn't precisely fit the easy/hard dichotomy you have set up, there's something to be said for "anything worth doing." Yeah, it would be spectacular if you could just flip a switch and game on Linux instead of Windows, but it's not like you have to recompile the kernel and hunt down modules like you did in the old days. I've even built a "big picture" Steam Machine for the living room, and it's turned out to be a pretty awesome investment.

The tools are there; you just have to use them.

Depends a lot on what you're planning to do with it; what your end-game is. I wouldn't start with Arch, personally, as it has a more true-Unix feel than most other Linux distributions. That said, if you like tinkering, and you want to get the absolute best out of your hardware, it's hands-down the best option. Just understand up-front that you'll probably be fiddling with it more than playing on it.

While all of my servers are running some form of FreeBSD, I try to stick with Ubuntu or a downstream distribution for workstations, largely to keep other household members happy and to ensure the greatest flexibility and cross-functionality. A lot of stuff these days, while it's clearly designed to run on any Linux distro with the right rereqs, is simply built on Ubuntu, so sticking with that or a downstream distro will preemptively quash a lot of bugs you could run across when setting things up for gaming.

I've tried to stick with Mint as much as possible, myself. In retrospect, I would probably have gone with a headless Ubuntu install for the HTPC and simply loaded a bare-bones DE to get Steam and Kodi working, but I'm already committed; no sense in starting over. It's something to consider if you're going the HTPC route, though, and don't want to load SteamOS.

On the hardware side, it's largely dealer's choice these days, as most distros come complete with a great deal of the consumer-level drivers and firmware already loaded. My most recent build needed to fit into a tiny space, so it had to be built around a low-power i5 on a MiniITX board, crammed into a cabinet no bigger than a VCR. The case supported three 2.5" drives, so I went with some cheap SATAIII options and striped them, since all that's going on it is game data that can always be re-installed.

The only thing you'll really need to be concerned about in any build, regardless of intent, is the GPU; and on that front, at least for the time being, you'll want to stick with NVidia. AMD/ATI has been making great strides in catching up to NVidia on the performance side of things, and there's even room to argue that you can get more bang for the buck shopping the former over the latter, but AMD has yet to put out decent third-party drivers for Linux, while NVidia's drivers continue to improve measurably on every release.

Anyway, I digress. Bottom line: stick with an Ubuntu downstream if you want to do more gaming than configuration; stick with low-power Intel components if you build small for cabinets or such; stick with NVidia GPUs until you hear otherwise on the AMD driver situation.
